title: Tool & Function Schemas (JSON Schema)
summary: A tool is exposed to a model as a JSON Schema: a name, a description, and a parameters object typing each argument. The model reads this schema to decide whether and how to call the tool, so the description quality directly drives selection accuracy, and the parameter types constrain what arguments come back. This topic covers writing good schemas by hand and generating them automatically from Python type hints and pydantic models.

subtopics.title: A tool schema has three parts
subtopics.explanation: Every tool the model can call is described by a JSON object with a name, a natural-language description, and a parameters object that is itself a JSON Schema. The name is the identifier your code dispatches on, the description tells the model when to use it, and the parameters declare each argument's type and whether it is required. Getting all three right is what lets the model both choose the tool and fill in valid arguments.

subtopics.title: The description is what the model reads to choose
subtopics.explanation: The model never sees your function body — it sees only the schema, and the description is the single biggest lever on whether it picks the right tool at the right time. A vague description ('does stuff with orders') causes wrong or missed calls; a precise one ('Look up a customer order by its id and return status and total') guides selection. Writing the description for the model, not for a human reader, is the highest-leverage skill in tool design.

subtopics.title: Typed parameters and enums constrain the arguments
subtopics.explanation: Each property in the parameters schema declares a type (string, number, integer, boolean, array, object) and can restrict values with an enum, so the model returns arguments your function can actually accept. Marking fields required prevents the model from omitting them, and enums stop it from inventing categories. Precise parameter typing is what turns 'roughly the right idea' into arguments you can pass straight into your function.

subtopics.title: Generate schemas from Python type hints
subtopics.explanation: Hand-writing JSON Schema is repetitive and drifts from the actual function signature, so a common pattern is to derive the schema from the function's type hints via inspection. You read the signature, map Python types to JSON Schema types, and pull the description from the docstring. Generating the schema from the source of truth — the function itself — keeps the contract and the code from silently diverging.

subtopics.title: Generate schemas from pydantic models
subtopics.explanation: Pydantic models already carry field types, constraints, and descriptions, and they expose `.model_json_schema()` to emit a JSON Schema for free. Defining your tool's arguments as a pydantic model gives you both validation of the incoming arguments and the schema you hand the model from one definition. Using pydantic as the single source of truth eliminates the gap between what you tell the model and what your code will actually accept.
subtopics.example:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class GetOrderArgs(BaseModel):
    order_id: str = Field(description="e.g. 'A-123'")
    include_items: bool = False

tool = {
    "name": "get_order",
    "description": "Look up an order by id.",
    "parameters": GetOrderArgs.model_json_schema(),  # schema for free
}
# same model also validates the args the model returns
args = GetOrderArgs(**{"order_id": "A-123"})

foundations.overview: When you give an agent a tool, the model never sees your code — it sees a JSON Schema describing the tool: a name it will echo back when it wants to call the tool, a natural-language description of what the tool does and when to use it, and a parameters object that is itself a JSON Schema typing each argument. The model uses the description to decide *whether* to call the tool and *which* one among many, and it uses the parameter types, enums, and required lists to construct valid arguments. This means schema quality is not cosmetic: a weak description causes the model to skip the tool or pick the wrong one, and loose parameter types produce arguments your function can't accept. Because writing and maintaining these schemas by hand is error-prone and drifts from the real signature, the practical move is to generate them from a single source of truth — Python type hints via inspection, or better, a pydantic model that both emits the schema (model_json_schema) and validates the arguments the model returns. Master the schema and you control both tool selection and argument correctness, the two things that determine whether an agent uses its tools well.
foundations.formalDefinition: A tool (function) schema is a JSON object with fields name (string identifier), description (natural-language spec of purpose and usage), and parameters (a JSON Schema of type 'object' whose properties type each argument, with an optional required array and per-property constraints such as enum, minimum, or maximum). It is passed to the model alongside the messages; the model returns tool calls naming a tool and supplying arguments intended to conform to its parameters schema.
foundations.whyItMatters: Tool selection and argument correctness are the two failure modes that make or break tool-using agents, and both are governed by the schema. Investing in clear descriptions and tight parameter types measurably raises the rate at which the model calls the right tool with valid arguments on the first try, cutting retries, wrong actions, and downstream validation failures.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of the schema as a job posting the model reads before applying. The name is the job title, the description is the responsibilities and when-to-apply section, and the parameters are the required-qualifications form with typed fields and dropdowns (enums). A vague posting attracts the wrong applicants (wrong tool) or none; a precise one gets exactly the candidate you want with a correctly filled form (valid arguments).
foundations.realWorldUsage: Every function-calling agent ships tool schemas: coding agents declare read_file/run_tests schemas, support agents declare get_order/issue_refund, data agents declare run_query with a typed SQL or parameter object. Teams increasingly generate these from pydantic models so the schema and the executing function never drift apart.
foundations.performanceImpact: Description clarity and parameter tightness raise first-try tool-selection and argument-validity rates, which reduces wasted turns (each a full model round-trip) and downstream retries. Very large schemas or dozens of tools inflate input tokens and can degrade selection, so keeping schemas lean and the tool set focused improves both accuracy and cost.

Improving tool-selection accuracy via better descriptions

commonMisconceptions.myth: The model sees my function code, so the description is just documentation.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The model sees only the schema, never the body. The description is the model's sole basis for choosing the tool, so it directly determines selection accuracy.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A JSON Schema on the parameters guarantees valid arguments.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It strongly guides the model but is not enforced by generation on every provider; you still validate the returned arguments (e.g. with pydantic) before executing.

commonMisconceptions.myth: More tools with rich schemas always help the model.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Too many tools or bloated schemas raise input tokens and can confuse selection. A focused set with tight schemas usually outperforms a sprawling one.

interactiveExamples.title: Generate a tool schema from a pydantic model
interactiveExamples.explanation: Define the tool's arguments once as a pydantic model with types, defaults, and field descriptions, then derive the JSON Schema automatically and reuse the same model to validate incoming arguments — one source of truth for both.

code.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from typing import Literal

class SearchArgs(BaseModel):
    query: str = Field(description="Free-text search query")
    limit: int = Field(default=10, ge=1, le=50, description="Max results")
    sort: Literal["relevance", "date"] = "relevance"

def tool_schema(name, description, args_model):
    return {
        "name": name,
        "description": description,
        "parameters": args_model.model_json_schema(),
    }

schema = tool_schema("search_docs", "Search the docs index.", SearchArgs)
props = schema["parameters"]["properties"]
print("types:", props["query"]["type"], props["limit"]["type"])
print("enum:", props["sort"]["enum"])

# same model validates what the model returns
valid = SearchArgs(**{"query": "agents", "limit": 5})
print("validated limit:", valid.limit)
code.caption: model_json_schema() turns the pydantic model into the parameters schema, and the same class validates the arguments the model sends back.
code.expectedOutput:
types: string integer
enum: ['relevance', 'date']
validated limit: 5

codeLab.title: Build a schema generator from type hints
codeLab.instructions: Implement schema_from_fn(fn) -> dict that inspects a function and returns a tool schema. It must: (1) set 'name' to fn.__name__; (2) set 'description' to the stripped docstring (or '' if none); (3) build a parameters object of type 'object' where each parameter becomes a property whose 'type' is mapped from its annotation (str→'string', int→'integer', float→'number', bool→'boolean', anything else→'string'); (4) put every parameter that has no default into the 'required' list. The harness checks the schema against a sample function.

    # Map annotations to JSON Schema types; params without a default are required.
    ...

codeLab.testHarness:
def get_order(order_id: str, limit: int = 10, verbose: bool = False):
    """Look up an order by id."""
    ...

s = schema_from_fn(get_order)
assert s["name"] == "get_order"
assert s["description"] == "Look up an order by id."
props = s["parameters"]["properties"]
assert props["order_id"]["type"] == "string"
assert props["limit"]["type"] == "integer"
assert props["verbose"]["type"] == "boolean"
assert s["parameters"]["required"] == ["order_id"]
print("all tests passed")
hints: inspect.signature(fn).parameters gives an ordered mapping of name -> Parameter.
A parameter is required when param.default is inspect.Parameter.empty.
Use a dict to map Python annotation types to JSON Schema type strings, defaulting to 'string'.

checkpoints.prompt: What does the model actually read when deciding whether to call a tool?
options: The tool's JSON Schema — name, description, and parameters
The return value of the function
The registry dict in your code
checkpoints.explanation: The model sees only the schema, never the implementation. The description in particular drives whether and which tool it selects, and the parameters constrain the arguments it returns.

checkpoints.prompt: The model keeps calling this tool with an invalid 'status'. What's the schema problem?
options: There is no enum constraining 'status', so the model invents values like 'in-progress'; add enum: ['open','shipped','closed']
checkpoints.explanation: Without an enum the model is free to invent status strings. Declaring status as an enum of the allowed values constrains the model to valid categories your function accepts.

checkpoints.prompt: What does this pydantic schema generation print for the 'sort' field?
checkpoints.code:
from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import Literal
class A(BaseModel):
    sort: Literal["asc", "desc"] = "asc"
print(A.model_json_schema()["properties"]["sort"]["enum"])
checkpoints.explanation: A Literal type becomes an enum in the generated JSON Schema, so the 'sort' property's enum is ['asc', 'desc'] — the same constraint you'd write by hand.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the pydantic call that produces the parameters schema for a tool.
checkpoints.explanation: pydantic's model_json_schema() emits a JSON Schema for the model's fields, which is exactly the shape the 'parameters' field of a tool expects.

theory.question: What is a tool/function schema, and why does the description matter so much?
theory.directAnswer: A tool schema is the JSON the model reads to use a tool: a name it echoes when calling, a description of what the tool does and when to use it, and a parameters JSON Schema typing each argument. The description matters most because the model never sees your code — it decides whether and which tool to call purely from the description, so a vague one causes missed or wrong calls while a precise one drives correct selection.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A JSON object (name, description, parameters) describing a callable to a function-calling model, where parameters is itself a JSON Schema with types, enums, and required fields.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The model cannot inspect your functions; it needs a machine- and model-readable contract to know what tools exist, when to use each, and how to shape arguments.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You pass the schemas alongside the messages; the model reads the descriptions to pick a tool and the parameter types/enums to build arguments, then returns a tool call your code validates and executes.

theory.whyImportant: Tool selection and argument validity — the two things that make tool use work — are both governed by the schema, so schema quality is a direct lever on agent accuracy and cost.
theory.realWorldExample: Renaming a support tool's description from 'gets data' to 'Look up a specific order by id and return status and total; use for questions about an existing order' sharply increased how often the model called it correctly instead of guessing.

followUps.question: Does the parameters schema guarantee valid arguments?
followUps.answer: It strongly guides the model but isn't enforced by every provider's generation, so you still validate returned arguments (e.g. with pydantic) before executing.

followUps.question: What happens if you register too many tools?
followUps.answer: Input tokens rise and selection can degrade; a focused set with tight schemas usually beats a large sprawling one.

theory.question: Why generate tool schemas from type hints or pydantic instead of hand-writing them?
theory.directAnswer: Because a hand-written schema drifts from the actual function signature over time — a renamed parameter or changed type silently breaks the contract. Generating the schema from the source of truth (type hints via inspection, or a pydantic model) keeps the schema and the executing code in lockstep, and pydantic additionally validates the arguments the model returns from that same definition.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Deriving the tool's JSON Schema programmatically from the function's signature or a pydantic args model rather than maintaining a separate hand-written schema.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Duplicated contracts drift; when the schema and the function disagree, the model sends arguments the function can't accept, causing silent runtime failures.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: For type hints, inspect the signature and map Python types to JSON Schema types and defaults to required-ness; for pydantic, call model_json_schema() for the parameters and reuse the model to validate incoming arguments.

theory.whyImportant: It eliminates the drift between what you tell the model and what your code accepts, which is a common and hard-to-spot source of tool-call failures.
theory.realWorldExample: A team defined each tool's arguments as a pydantic model, generated the schema from it, and validated calls with it; when they added a required field, both the model-facing schema and the validation updated from one edit.

followUps.question: What does pydantic add beyond schema generation?
followUps.answer: It validates and coerces the arguments the model returns (types, ranges, enums) before you execute, catching bad calls at a clear boundary.

followUps.question: A limitation of the inspection approach?
followUps.answer: Simple type maps miss complex types (unions, nested objects, constraints); pydantic handles those far better and should be preferred for non-trivial arguments.

scenario.question: Your agent has ten tools and frequently calls the wrong one or skips the right one. How do you improve selection?
scenario.directAnswer: Treat it as a schema-quality problem. Audit descriptions so each states precisely what the tool does, when to use it, and what it returns, and disambiguate overlapping tools. Tighten parameters with types and enums so mis-selected calls fail validation loudly, prune or merge redundant tools to shrink the choice set and input tokens, and add a few-shot example or system hint for genuinely ambiguous cases. Measure per-tool selection accuracy before and after.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A tool-selection accuracy problem driven by weak or overlapping schemas and an over-large tool set.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The model picks tools solely from descriptions; vague or near-duplicate descriptions and too many options make the choice ambiguous, so it guesses.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Rewrite descriptions to be specific and mutually distinct, add enums/required fields so wrong arguments are caught, reduce the tool count, and instrument selection accuracy per tool to verify the fix.

scenario.whyImportant: It shows that selection errors are usually fixable in the schema layer, not by changing models, and ties description quality directly to agent correctness.
scenario.realWorldExample: Two tools, 'search' and 'lookup', had near-identical vague descriptions; clarifying that 'search' is for free-text discovery and 'lookup' is for a known id, plus removing three unused tools, roughly halved wrong-tool calls.

followUps.question: How do you decide whether to merge two tools?
followUps.answer: If they take the same inputs and the model confuses them, merge into one tool with a parameter that selects the mode; if they truly differ, sharpen the descriptions instead.

followUps.question: Why can fewer tools help?
followUps.answer: A smaller, well-separated tool set lowers ambiguity and input tokens, both of which improve first-try selection.

coding.question: Write a function that turns a Python function's signature and docstring into a tool JSON Schema.
coding.thoughtProcess: The signature is the source of truth, so I inspect it, map each annotation to a JSON Schema type with a sensible string default, and mark parameters that lack a default as required. The docstring becomes the description. This keeps the schema and function from drifting, and callers can extend the type map for richer types later.
lineByLine: PY_TO_JSON maps Python annotation types to JSON Schema type strings.
inspect.signature gives an ordered view of the function's parameters.
Each parameter becomes a property; unknown annotations fall back to 'string'.
A missing default (inspect.Parameter.empty) marks the parameter as required.
The docstring is stripped into the description the model will read.
The result is a ready-to-pass tool schema derived entirely from the function.
coding.timeComplexity: O(p) in the number of parameters.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(p) for the properties and required list.

followUps.question: How would you support enums or ranges?
followUps.answer: Switch to pydantic: use Literal for enums and Field(ge=..., le=...) for ranges, then emit model_json_schema() instead of hand-mapping types.

followUps.question: How do you keep the description high quality?
followUps.answer: Write the docstring for the model — state what the tool does, when to use it, and what it returns — since that text is exactly what drives selection.

keyTakeaways: A tool schema is name + description + a parameters JSON Schema; the model reads only this, never your code.
The description drives tool selection — write it for the model: what the tool does, when to use it, what it returns.
Typed parameters, enums, and required fields constrain the arguments the model returns to what your function accepts.
Generate schemas from the source of truth (type hints or pydantic) so the contract can't drift from the function.
A JSON Schema guides but doesn't guarantee valid arguments — validate returned arguments (e.g. pydantic) before executing.
